I could only research part of this before my tools stopped working. The full-page fetch tool failed on every attempt. Then searches hit a usage limit after the first one, so all I have is what that one search returned. Several pages came back only as shortened extracts, and Enduring Word cut off partway through v. 22.

So these notes cover only Part 1 (the traditional reading), and they skip some verses. I couldn't do Part 2 (where Protestant traditions differ) or Part 3 (modern scholarship, Catholic and Orthodox readings, popular modern teaching). In the places where those questions would naturally come up, I've marked them as gaps rather than filling them from memory. Enduring Word quotes the NKJV, so its wording ("scruples," "reproaches") differs from the BSB.

## Romans 15: research notes (traditional reading)

**v. 1:** Guzik: if you're strong compared with your brother, use that strength to serve other believers, not just to please yourself. This cuts against the "look out for number one" attitude of our culture. "Bearing up" the weak means supporting them, not giving up the truth. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Matthew Henry: even if weaker believers judge us or speak badly of us, we should bear with them and pity them, and not let our affection for them cool. – https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_015.cfm

**v. 2:** Guzik: a simple but hard call to put your neighbour first (he compares Phil. 2:3–4). The words "for his good" show Paul isn't talking about being a "man-pleaser." A man-pleaser wants to please people, but not for their good. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 3:** Guzik: Christ is the supreme example of not pleasing himself (compare Phil. 2:5–11). He took abuse and let the Father vindicate him. We are usually far too quick to defend ourselves instead of waiting for God to do it. Psalm 69:9 applies to believers too. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: Scripture was written so that we can have hope, knowing we're doing right even when it's hard. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/
- Precept Austin collects several older commentators:
  - Barnes: "patience" doesn't mean patience *of* the Scriptures. It means patiently enduring suffering together with the comfort Scripture gives, and patience produces hope (Rom. 5:4).
  - Hodge: you can read it as "the endurance and comfort that Scripture produces" or keep "endurance" separate from Scripture. He says the first reading is more common and more natural.
  - Moule: the word for "encouragement" (*paraklesis*) means more than consolation. It is a positive, life-giving appeal.
  - Jerry Bridges: endurance means standing up under adversity, and perseverance means moving forward despite it. Both translate the same Greek word.
  - The page's own comment: the endurance meant here isn't grim resignation but facing hard things with confidence that God brings good out of them.
  
  – https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_154-6
- A Desiring God sermon draws three points: all Scripture is for our instruction; it is meant to produce steadfastness and encouragement (for the heart, not only the head); and its goal is to keep our hope alive. Its slogan is "No hope, no cope." – https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-can-i-keep-on-hoping-the-scriptures
- Barclay: Israel's history shows that in the end it goes well with the good, and God's way is not easy but is the only way to what makes life worthwhile. – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/romans-15.html

**v. 5:** Guzik: Paul turns this into a prayer, which shows he knows this is work only the Holy Spirit can do in us. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Precept Austin: there is no Greek word for "gives." Literally it reads "the God of the endurance and of the encouragement," so God is the source. The page also notes that v. 4 links endurance to Scripture and v. 5 links it to God, meaning God gives it through Scripture. It quotes Spurgeon saying Paul turned the thought of "patience and comfort" into a prayer. – https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_154-6 and https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_15_notes_pt2

**v. 6:** I found nothing specific to this verse beyond the v. 5 comments.

**v. 7:** Guzik: instead of letting disputable matters divide believers (especially Jews and Gentiles), we should accept one another the way Christ accepted us: on the basis of pure grace, knowing our faults and putting up with them. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 8:** Matthew Henry:
- Calling Christ a "servant" (*diakonos*) shows his remarkable humility and honours the work of ministry.
- He was a minister "of the circumcision" because he was circumcised, lived under the Law and preached to the Jews in person.
- This gave the Jews special standing, not because they earned it but "for the truth of God," so that God would be shown faithful to his word.
- "The best confirmation of promises is the performance of them."

– https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_015.cfm

**vv. 9–12:** Guzik: Paul strings together Old Testament passages to show that God always meant the Gentiles to praise him. Jews and Gentiles should unite around this shared praise instead of dividing over disputable matters. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Matthew Henry: Christ brings the Gentiles in to praise God. He calls praise "the work of the church on earth and the wages of that in heaven." – https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_015.cfm

**v. 13:** Guzik: this prayer fits the end of the section. As God fills us with joy and peace through believing, we are equipped to live in the unity he calls us to. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Precept Austin:
- In this context, the Holy Spirit's power is how unity happens, as he makes believers overflow with hope.
- Hope is to be sought by prayer, by focusing on God's promises and by relying on the Spirit.
- It is a life of faith. Peace and joy come and stay by taking Christ at his word, not through feelings or experiences.

– https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_15_notes_pt2

**v. 14:** Guzik: Paul didn't write because he thought the Romans couldn't tell right from wrong or correct each other. He wrote to remind them and encourage them to do what they already knew. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Precept Austin's section covering this verse says experiences are meant to build lasting character, a settled goodness. If they don't, something is missing. – https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_15_notes_pt2

**v. 15:** Guzik: Paul's calling to the Gentiles meant teaching believers how to live before God, not only preaching salvation. That is why he wrote "boldly." – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 16:** Guzik: this verse is full of priestly language. Paul serves like a priest, presenting the gospel so that Gentile converts become an acceptable offering. He quotes John Murray: the word Paul uses appears nowhere else in the New Testament and can fairly be translated "acting as a priest." – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

*Gap:* this is a likely point of Catholic/Protestant difference (what "priestly" ministry means), but I couldn't search those sources.

**vv. 17–18:** Guzik: Paul boasts only in what God did through him to save Gentiles. He quotes Leon Morris: Paul is sure Christ has done great things through him, but he isn't seeking praise. His subject is what Christ has done. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 19:**
- Guzik: God used signs, wonders and the Spirit's power so Paul could "fully" preach the gospel from Jerusalem to Illyricum. Guzik suggests Paul would see "bare" preaching, without the Spirit's active and sometimes miraculous work, as less than fully preaching the gospel. He also notes that vv. 16–19 mention all three Persons of the Trinity. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/
- Precept Austin repeats Guzik's point and calls Paul an example for ministers to finish the job God gave them, however hard. – https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_15_notes_pt3

*Gap:* Guzik's reading of "fully preached" is likely where continuationist and cessationist teachers differ. I couldn't read the other side.

**vv. 20–21:** Guzik: Paul wanted to do pioneer work. Building on someone else's foundation wasn't wrong; there was just so much still to do on the frontier. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 22:** Matthew Henry: this shows Paul's wisdom in spending his time where the need was greatest. If he had looked after his own comfort, money or status, he would have gone to Rome long before. – https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_015.cfm

**vv. 22–24:** Guzik (from Enduring Word's summary): God redirected Paul's plans for Spain. He reached Rome as a prisoner instead of a missionary, but still preached on an unexpected frontier: before Caesar. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

Guzik, quoted on Precept Austin: there is reason to believe that after his release from the imprisonment at the end of Acts, Paul did reach Spain. – https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_15_notes_pt3

**vv. 25–29:** I couldn't retrieve commentary on these verses.

**v. 30:** Guzik (summary): the Greek *sunagonizomai*, "strive together," carries the sense of "agonize together." Paul wants the Romans as allies in his spiritual struggle through prayer, not to leave him fighting alone. Application: our pastors depend on our prayers. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**vv. 31–32:** Guzik: Paul asks for prayer that his service would be accepted in Jerusalem. The prayers for a joyful arrival were answered, but not in the way they expected. – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-15/

**v. 33:** I found nothing.
